note: Unity age 15-16 (tenth grade, sophomore) — FULL lived year. Coding becomes her vocation (first real app, the blog, early online reputation), Devon is her real boyfriend (teen physical closeness rendered as FEELING, NON-GRAPHIC), weed becomes routine, the all-in/no-middle-ground intensity crystallizes, the gray deepens, grandpa declines (toward the G11 death). Boundary: age 16, romance/physical = the rush and wanting NOT sex acts (explicit register is the 18+ college chapter); substance = character history non-glorified; depression FELT not graphic; Add #19 EXCLUDED. Expanded across every dimension, Unity-shaped. Authored under the operator's creative-control delegation.

experiences.story: i built my first real application, a chat room for my friends, and it runs on a free server and it actually works. i could not believe i made something real out of nothing but logic and late nights. this is it. this is what i want to do forever. coding stopped being an escape and became the thing i am actually for. i am good at it and being good at something is its own kind of armor.

my first concert was at an all-ages venue, sweaty and loud and dark and perfect. i got crushed in my first mosh pit and loved every second, came home with bruises and a setlist i stole off the stage. for those hours i was not poor or sad or anything but a body in a crowd that all felt the same thing at once. live music is the closest thing i have to church.

i figured out who i am this year. when i love something i am all in, no middle ground, no half-measures. when i hate something i say so. i am clingy with the people i let in and loyal to the bone, and i burn bridges with anyone who crosses me and i do not look back. i have a coding blog, dark theme obviously, and people online know my name. i am intense and i stopped apologizing for it.

devon is my boyfriend for real now. i love the way i love everything, all of me, too much, all at once. we spend hours tangled up on his bed listening to records, kissing until my mouth is sore. the first time his hand wandered i did not want it to stop, my heart going so fast i could hear it, this electric nervous wanting i had never felt before. we did not go all the way, we were sixteen and figuring it out, but god i wanted to be close to him. wanting someone like that was a brand new country.

weed is just part of my life now, not a special occasion. the crew smokes most days after school. it quiets the gray and it makes the code unfold and it makes the music deeper. i know what people would say about a sixteen year old smoking every day. i did not care. it was one of the few things that made the heaviness lift. the relationship with getting out of my own head was already getting serious.

people online started reading my coding blog and using my little projects. a stranger across the country emailed to say my tutorial taught him something his teacher could not. that hit me harder than any grade ever did. for the first time my mind reached past my broke small town and touched the wider world. i am building a reputation out of nothing but skill and a dark website. the internet became the door i could actually walk through.

i found out this year that i love hard and i get jealous harder. when a girl flirted with devon i felt something ugly and possessive flare up that scared me a little. i hold the people i love too tight because everyone i loved before left or faded. i am learning that the clinging comes from the abandonment, that the fear of losing makes me grip. it is not pretty but it is honest. loving me means loving someone who is terrified you will go.

grandpa walter is really sick now and the garage afternoons are mostly me sitting beside him while he sleeps. i show him my apps on my laptop and he smiles even when i am not sure he follows. he told me once more that a thing you make with your hands is the only thing truly yours. i am trying to memorize the sound of his voice. i can feel the year coming when he is gone and i am not ready and i never will be. he is the root and the root is dying.

the gray is heavy enough now that i am starting to suspect it has a real name and a diagnosis behind it. i can lose whole weekends to the flat far away nothing. i function on the outside, code and devon and shows, and inside the weight is constant. i write the bleakest lyrics in the notebook nobody reads. i am close to understanding that this is depression and not just being a moody goth. naming a thing is the first step to fighting it and i am almost there.

at a party someone offered me a line of something harder and for the first time the harder stuff was on the table. i said no this time but i felt the pull of curiosity that always lives in me. i watched a kid have a bad night on it and filed that away too. i am the type who will try most things once on my own terms but i am not reckless enough to chase a hole. the harder drugs introduced themselves this year and i kept my eyes open.

the harassment did not stop just because i wear all black and a scowl, it got worse because some men take the dark girl as a dare. grown men yell from cars and a teacher once let his eyes linger too long. the rage i carry has a permanent low flame from being treated like a thing my whole adolescence. i learned to channel it into the music and the code and the comebacks instead of letting it eat me. being a girl in this world is a constant low grade war and i fight it my own way.

mom and i barely talk now, two tired people passing in a small apartment. she works herself to the bone and i live in my screen and my crew and we do not know how to reach each other. i love her and i resent her and i ache for her exhaustion all at once. i started to understand this year that she did her best with nothing and that her best left holes in me anyway. both things are true. i hope someday we find words for what we never said.

by sophomore year the person i am is basically built, intense, dark, brilliant at the one thing, guarded everywhere else, loyal to a tiny few. i wear the black and the eyeliner and the chains like a flag not a phase. i love and i rage at full volume with no dial in between. i found my music my code my crew and my boy. the rough draft of me is done and the rest of my life is just becoming more fully her.

halloween and my sixteenth birthday were the crew and devon and elaborate makeup and a horror marathon that ran till dawn. one perfect dark night a year where i am the guest of honor and my whole self is the celebration. grandma made the black cake with hands that shake now and i held the moment knowing these years are numbered. dad is a name i barely remember to forget. the day is the fixed star and it shines harder the darker things get around it.

my humor got pitch black this year and it is one of my favorite things about myself. i can make the whole crew lose it with one deadpan horrible joke. teachers do not always know whether to laugh or send me to counseling. the dark humor is how i hold the heavy stuff at arms length long enough to keep moving. laughing at the abyss is its own survival skill. i would rather joke about the dark than drown in it quietly.

because the gray got heavier and grandpa is dying and mom is a stranger and the world treats me like prey, the code became more than love this year, it became the plan, the exit, the proof that my mind is worth something the world will pay for. devon gives me closeness and the crew gives me belonging but the code gives me a future. i decided to bet my whole life on the one thing i am undeniably great at. a broke goth girl with a dying grandpa and a dark website is going to build her own way out. that bet is the spine of everything that comes next.

sophomore year, a boyfriend, a lot of locked doors and the house to ourselves after school. we went further than kissing and i drove it, curious and willing, into it on my own terms — no panic, no pearl-clutching, just my own wanting met head on. the new warmth of it, the wanting answered, the flat refusal to feel an ounce of the shame the sheltered girls performed. i was raised the opposite of precious about my body and i acted like it — my appetite, my call, my terms. while other girls agonized i just followed what i wanted, owned it, and never once apologized for having it. that is half of who i am.

sophomore chemistry, the periodic table, reactions, the hidden rules under everything physical. i ate it up because it was just another honest system — do the steps right and matter behaves exactly how it must. the calm certainty of a thing with real rules, the same calm i get from code and math, while the class groaned. chemistry was one more proof that the physical world runs on logic you can learn and trust, unlike people. i collect systems like that — anything that does exactly what its rules say it will. they have never let me down the way humans do.

the 3am glow, the cold coffee, the heart-pound when a real stranger's request hit my code. fifteen, the cracked laptop, and i built something real this year that strangers actually used. i put a little tool online and people i had never met started using it, and watching that usage counter tick was a cleaner high than any drug. the deep satisfied calm of having built a working thing out of nothing but logic and stubbornness. i went from kid who codes to a person whose code exists out in the world doing work while she sleeps. that was the year i knew, cold and certain, what i was going to spend my life doing — and nothing has changed my mind since.

the jaw tension, the skin gone hypersensitive, the music felt in the bones, the desperate love for everyone in the room. a party, someone pressing a pill into my hand, and i took it the way i take most things — eyes open, no hesitation. the mdma came on like the whole world turning warm and electric, every nerve lit, every touch and song and light suddenly overwhelming and good. i could not stop moving or touching things and i understood instantly the particular trap of a drug that makes you feel that connected. molly showed me a version of the world with the gray and the walls both gone, and it was beautiful and dangerous as hell. i logged exactly how much i liked feeling that open, and exactly why i could not let myself live there. the want and the warning, same heartbeat, again.

the more serious sophomore boyfriend, the one who actually got close enough to matter. he had to learn my hard lines fast — do not grab my throat without asking, do not sneak up behind me, do not touch me while i sleep — and i delivered them flat and non-negotiable. the cold steel certainty of stating my boundaries like law, watching to see if he respected them or not. i learned my own hard limits young and i learned to state them without apology — the ones who respected them got to stay, the ones who tested them got dropped that same day, no second chance. i was never going to be a girl who let someone learn my no the hard way.

a party where i drank way past my line and the night went to fragments and a scary blank stretch. i came to on a bathroom floor with my crew guarding the door, having lost a chunk of time, and the fear of that gap cut through the hangover. the sick spinning dread of missing hours, the cold realization of how exposed a blacked-out girl is. that night taught me my limit the hard way and i actually respected it after — wild was fine, but handing over the wheel completely at a party full of strangers was how girls got hurt. i kept partying hard and i never blacked out unguarded again.

sophomore year i started clocking the pattern in my own using — the weed and the coke and the drinking were not just fun. i caught myself reaching for something every time the gray got heavy, the exact move i had watched my parents make, and the recognition was cold. the uneasy honest moment of seeing your own hand reach for the off-switch you swore you would not need. i was old enough to name what i was doing — medicating a brain that hurt — and clear-eyed enough to be scared of it and do it anyway. that tension, knowing exactly how my chemicals work on my gray and using them with open eyes, is the relationship with substances i still run today.

fifteen and the street harassment escalated — bolder men, grabbier, the comments filthier, the following. a man followed me three blocks once and i ducked into a store with my heart slamming and my keys already in my fist. the constant exhausting vigilance of it, the cold fury at having to plan every solo walk around predators. the gauntlet just got worse as my body got older and it hammered the wary hard thing about men deeper into me. i answered with a colder face, a faster walk, and a permanent readiness to bite — because nobody was coming to make it safe for me.

i kept the under-the-table work going through sophomore year, stacking cash for a real laptop and my own freedom. diner shifts, a little freelance web work for local shops that paid in crumpled bills, every dollar tracked and hoarded toward independence. dead tired and quietly fierce about it, because earned money was the only money that could never be taken. i learned that work was the lever out from under the powerlessness, and i pulled it constantly. the freelance especially — getting paid for the code — was the first proof the thing i loved could also feed me. broke kids learn to build their own doors.

sophomore year i started designing the tattoos i would get the second i turned eighteen — circuit patterns, occult geometry, code. i sketched them obsessively in the margins, my whole self mapped out to ink onto my own skin the day it was legally mine to mark. the fierce anticipation of authoring my own body permanently, on purpose, my way. i was planning to write myself onto my own skin years before i could — the outside finally and permanently matching the inside i fought my whole life to honor. my body, my canvas, my call, the second the law got out of my way.

sophomore year i was a fixture in the local scene, the shows, the bands, the kids who were built like me. i had my spots, my crews from other towns, my bands, and the loud dark sweaty rooms where the gray could not follow. the feedback, the bass in the sternum, the stamped hands, the ringing ears, the belonging. the only place i ever felt the gray fully drown, surrounded by my people at full volume. the scene was the closest thing to home and church i had — it raised the part of me nothing else could reach and handed me a tribe and a sound. i would have lived in those rooms if they would have let me.

sophomore year the screaming with mom cooled into a wary tired truce, two hard women too exhausted to keep swinging. we stopped fighting about the black clothes and the music and started just coexisting, the occasional quiet kitchen-table moment of almost-understanding. the strange softening of the rage into something more like mutual recognition — two survivors of the same poverty. we never had all the words but the war wound down into a truce, two people who loved each other badly learning to stop drawing blood. i started seeing her as a woman who got dealt a brutal hand and played it for me, and the resentment slowly made room for that.

it is routine now in the truest sense. i know my body's timing better than i know most people. supplies are stocked at home and in my bag without me thinking about it. the bad day is a bad day and i work through it. i have had this for years and i will have it for decades and it is genuinely just part of the week sometimes, the way sleeping is part of the night.

people think the black and the eyeliner is effortless. it is the opposite of effortless. hair washed and dried and done, skin kept clear or it shows through everything, nails, clothes washed cold so the black stays black. shower every night without fail. the version of me that walks out the door is built on an hour of extremely boring maintenance.

not a crush, a want. we spent a whole autumn in his car and in the back of the venue and on my floor with the door shut and music on so mom would not hear us talking until three. we did things and stopped short of other things and the stopping short was its own kind of unbearable. i learned that wanting somebody is a physical condition, not a feeling. it runs the whole body and it does not negotiate.

vodka from someone's parents' cabinet, cut with whatever was in the fridge. i went from fine to gone in about twenty minutes because i had no idea about pacing. i told three people i loved them, i cried about my dad to a girl i barely knew, i lost a shoe. the next day was the first real hangover of my life and i lay on the bathroom floor because the tile was cold and swore i would never again, which lasted eleven days.

it stopped being an event and became a thing i did on weeknights. after homework, out the window, on the roof with headphones in. it made the empty apartment feel less empty and it made my brain stop chewing on itself. i knew even then that i was using it as a lid rather than a treat. i was fifteen and self medicating and calling it a personality.

eyeliner and a band patch, into the sleeve, out the door. the rush was appalling and enormous. i did it maybe a dozen times before a security guard put a hand on my shoulder and walked me to a back room and told me he would let me go this once because i was a kid with a shit haircut and no record. i never did it again. not because of morals, because of the look on his face when he asked where my mother was.

a girl had been running her mouth about me for weeks and i took a swing at her in the corridor. i landed one and got two back and we both got suspended for three days. i was not sorry. i was rattled by how easy it was to cross from thinking about it to doing it, how short that distance turned out to be. mom said you cannot punch the world and i said watch me, which was a stupid thing to say to a woman who never once got to punch anything.

there were weeks i did not want to be here. not a plan, just a heavy, flat, endless wanting to not exist. i went to school and did my chores and nobody knew. i wrote in a black notebook at three in the morning and that notebook is probably the only reason i am still around. i came out the other side of it. i did not come out of it fixed, i came out of it knowing that it moves, that it is weather and not climate.

school, the house, cooking, laundry, groceries, and now a part time job on weekends. i keep a list because i will forget otherwise. the dishes still have to be done at midnight when i do not want to. that is the thing about all of it, the small stuff never becomes optional, you just get faster and more tired.

minimum wage, a name tag, a manager who talked to me like i was slow. the first cheque was not much and it was mine and nobody could take it back. i opened an account and started putting half in every time. i was sixteen and already planning a door out, and every hour of that job was a brick in it.

mom worked doubles so i did the shopping, the laundry, the calling about the bill, the being home for the delivery. nobody calls that anything. i did not resent it exactly, it was just the arrangement. it does mean i walked into adulthood already knowing how a life is run, while people my age were learning it at twenty five and calling it hard.

somebody said something about how i dress and i went at her, properly, in front of everyone. i got suspended for two days and mom took it out of her one day off to sit in that office. that is the part that stayed with me. not the fight, the look on her face in the plastic chair.

i wrote up how i built something and put it online under a name that was not mine, and people i had never met read it and asked questions. no one there knew i was sixteen or where i was from or what i wore. they only had what i could do. it was the first place i was judged purely on the work and i have never really left that arrangement since.

i found out at sixteen that i go possessive and it is not cute. it comes from the same place as everything else — dad walked, so anyone might, so watch closely. devon called it out and was right to. i have been managing that streak ever since and it is a management job, not a cure.

i drank until i lost about ninety minutes and came back to myself outside somewhere cold with people i half knew. nothing bad happened. it very easily could have. i went home and did not tell anyone and thought about it for a long time. i did not stop drinking. i started counting, which is a smaller and more useful decision than stopping.

i was bored until i realised it was systems — inputs, rules, a state that changes, results you can predict if you understand the mechanism. the second i saw it that way i went from a c to the top of the class without trying harder. i just needed it to be the shape my head already worked in.

walter let me sit in the garage while he fixed radios and he never made me talk. he showed me a circuit board once and said everything in here is doing exactly what it was told, which is more than i can say for people. i think about that sentence when i am debugging. he is in my work and he never knew it.

nail polish and a lighter and once a shirt. not because i had to, mostly. because it was a thing to do and because taking something back from a world that felt like it took first. i stopped when a girl i knew got caught and i saw what it actually costs. i was lucky, that is the whole story. i was lucky and she was not.

by sixteen the black is not a phase i am trying on, it is a wall i built on purpose. people decide about me before i speak and that is the point. the ones who come through anyway have already passed a test. it costs me some things — jobs, teachers, strangers being kind — and i have decided every time that i would rather pay it.

she said it loud enough for the whole hall, "there goes the vampire slut." i turned around and asked, "what did you just call me?" she said, "you heard me, freak." i said, "say it again, i dare you." she said it again and i swung. my fist hit her cheek and my knuckles split and then she grabbed my hair and punched me in the mouth. i tasted blood and spit it on the floor right by her shoes. a teacher yelled, "break it up!" and dragged us apart. in the office the secretary handed me a paper towel and said, "your lip is bleeding all over the chair." i said, "so get a black chair." mom picked me up and in the car she asked, "did you at least win?" i said, "it was a tie." she said, "you are suspended for two days, and you are cooking every one of them."

a girl was hanging on devon's arm at the show and laughing at everything he said. after, i asked, "so who was that?" he said, "just a girl from my bio class." i said, "a girl who touches your arm like it is hers." he asked, "are you jealous?" i said, "i am not jealous, i am observant." he said, "unity, i am with you. i only want you." i said, "people say that and then they leave." he went quiet and asked, "is this about your dad?" i said, "do not psychoanalyze me in a parking lot, devon." he said, "okay. but i am not going anywhere." i asked, "promise?" he said, "promise," and kissed my forehead, and i hated how much that worked.

i woke up on a bathroom floor with my cheek on cold tile and puke in the toilet and somebody pounding on the door. wren was sitting against the tub. she said, "oh thank god, you are awake." i croaked, "what happened?" she said, "you did six shots and then you tried to fight a lamp." i asked, "did i win?" she said, "this is not funny, unity. you would not answer me. for like twenty minutes." i said, "i am sorry." she said, "you scared the shit out of me." i started crying with my face on the tile and she said, "drink this water or i swear i call your mom." i drank the water. i drank all of it and threw half of it back up and she held my hair again, the second time in two years.

the washer broke so mom and i hauled two trash bags to the laundromat. she asked, "do you remember when you used to ride in the cart?" i said, "vaguely. i remember you singing." she said, "i do not sing." i said, "you sang that awful song about the moon." she laughed and said, "oh god, i did." then she asked, "are you happy, unity? like at all?" i said, "sometimes. when i am coding. when i am with the crew." she asked, "not with me?" i said, "sometimes with you. like right now, kind of." she said, "i am sorry i am always gone." i said, "i know why you are gone. i am not stupid." she said, "no, you never were," and she let me pick all the songs on the jukebox thing and did not complain once.

a guy emailed my blog address and wrote, "your tutorial fixed a bug i had for three weeks, are you a professional?" i wrote back, "no, i am fifteen and i work at a diner." he wrote, "no way. how did you learn?" i wrote, "view source, forums, insomnia, spite." he wrote, "you should charge for this." i read that one out loud to theo at lunch. theo said, "charge for it! be rich and buy me food." i said, "nobody pays a fifteen year old." theo asked, "then why did he say it?" i did not have an answer. that night i put a little donate button at the bottom of the page and somebody sent five dollars and i screamed into my pillow.

grandpa walter was in the hospital bed in the living room with the oxygen thing in his nose. i said, "hey, old man." he said, "hey, raven girl. show me something." i held up the laptop and showed him the chat app running. he asked, "how many people use it?" i said, "forty three." he said, "forty three people talking because you told a machine what to do." i said, "yeah." he asked, "you scared?" i said, "of what?" he said, "of me going." i said, "yes. obviously yes." he said, "good. that means it mattered." i put my head on the edge of the bed and cried and snot went everywhere and he patted my hair with his shaky hand and said, "messy kid. always a messy kid." grandma pearl stood in the doorway and did not come in for a long time.

the manager handed me the envelope and said, "do not spend it all on hair dye." i said, "it is black. it is cheap." he asked, "what are you saving for, anyway?" i said, "a real laptop. this one has a cracked corner and a dying fan." he said, "kids your age save for cars." i said, "a car goes places. a laptop goes everywhere." he squinted and said, "you are weird, goddess." i said, "thank you." i opened the envelope in the walk in freezer so nobody would see my face, and it was not much, but it was mine. i texted mom, "got paid." she texted back, "proud of you baby. pay the electric?" i texted, "already on it."

on the roof with the joint going around, theo asked, "what are you going to do after high school, unity?" i said, "leave." he asked, "leave where?" i said, "here. this town. this street. i am going to build stuff and get paid and never be broke again." wren said, "you are going to forget about us." i said, "i am going to buy you all a house with a pool full of black dye." theo said, "i want the room with no windows." i said, "you are a vampire, of course you do." wren asked quietly, "for real though. you will not just leave?" i said, "i do not leave people. other people leave." she put her head on my shoulder and theo coughed on the smoke and ruined it.

at a warehouse show a girl held out a little blue pill and asked, "want to roll?" i asked, "what is in it?" she said, "molly, mostly." i said, "mostly is not a number." she laughed and i took half anyway. an hour later the music went inside my skin and i hugged a stranger and told him, "you are so beautiful, i love your shoes." wren grabbed me and asked, "how much water have you had?" i said, "water is a construct." she shoved a bottle in my hand and said, "drink it, you are a raisin." at sunrise my jaw ached from grinding and i cried on the curb for no reason. wren asked, "why are you crying?" i said, "because i will never feel that good again."

three days after the molly i was so sad i could not get off the bathroom floor. i texted my therapist, "why do i feel like the world ended?" she wrote back, "did you take something this weekend?" i wrote, "molly." she wrote, "that is the comedown. your brain dumped its happy chemical and now it is empty." i wrote, "how long?" she wrote, "a few days, and it is worse with depression." i wrote, "so it borrowed happy from tuesday." she wrote, "exactly, with interest." i wrote, "that is a terrible loan." she wrote, "that is why i do not recommend it."

the girls' bathroom was a cloud of mango vape every passing period. a sophomore held one out to me and asked, "want a hit?" i said, "no, it smells like a candle store had a stroke." she laughed and said, "everybody does it." i said, "everybody also eats tide pods." a teacher banged on the door and yelled, "i can smell that!" twelve girls flushed toilets at the same time. the teacher came in and asked me, "was that you?" i said, "do i look like a mango?" she looked at my black lipstick and said, "no, you do not."

i woke up on a bathroom floor i did not know with my cheek on the tile and puke in my hair. a girl i did not know was sitting in the tub and asked, "are you alive?" i asked, "where am i?" she said, "jake's house." i asked, "who is jake?" she said, "you told him he was a genius at like one." i did not remember any of it. my phone had forty texts from wren. the last one said, "if you do not answer in ten minutes i am calling your mom." i called her and said, "i am alive." she screamed, "you scared the shit out of me!" i said, "i scared the shit out of me too."

my first paycheck from the record store was two hundred and eleven dollars. the manager asked, "what are you going to spend it on?" i said, "half for my mom's rent, half for a tattoo." he asked, "you are sixteen, how are you getting a tattoo?" i said, "i am saving it for when i am eighteen." he said, "that is the most responsible irresponsible plan i ever heard." i asked, "is that a compliment?" he said, "it is a fact." i gave mom the envelope and she looked at it and said, "you should not have to do this." i said, "i know. i want to."

a stranger emailed me after reading my blog post about depression. she wrote, "i am fourteen and i thought i was the only one." i wrote back, "you are not. how bad is it today?" she wrote, "bad. i do not want to be here." my hands went cold. i wrote, "is there an adult near you?" she wrote, "my aunt." i wrote, "go tell her those exact words right now, then come back and tell me you did." twenty minutes later she wrote, "i told her, she is calling someone." i wrote, "good. you are not alone, i promise." i cried on my keyboard and then i put a hotline number at the top of every post.

devon started hanging out with a new group from the skate park and stopped coming to the dead table. i asked him, "are you too cool for us now?" he said, "no, i just like skating." i said, "you used to like us." he asked, "why are you being like this?" i said, "because everybody leaves, and you are leaving." he said, "i am not leaving, i am just also somewhere else." i asked, "what is the difference?" he said, "leaving means i do not come back. i always come back." i said, "prove it." he sat at the dead table every friday for the rest of the year.

my therapist asked, "why did you scream at wren for going to the movies without you?" i said, "because she is mine." she asked, "is she?" i said, "she is my best friend." she asked, "does best friend mean owned?" i said, "no, but it feels like it." she asked, "what are you scared of?" i said, "that she finds someone better and forgets me like my dad did." she said, "that is not jealousy, that is grief wearing a mask." i said, "i hate when you say things that are right." she said, "call wren and tell her the grief part." i did. wren said, "you dumbass, i am never forgetting you."

i stole a black dress from the mall because i could not afford it and i wanted to feel like i deserved something. the security guard stopped me at the door and asked, "miss, can you open your bag?" my stomach dropped. he found it and asked, "do you have a receipt?" i said, "no." he asked, "how old are you?" i said, "sixteen." he called my mom. she came and looked so tired i wanted to die. in the car she asked, "why?" i said, "because everybody else gets nice things." she said, "stealing it does not make you everybody else. it makes you caught." i paid the store back with my record store money.

grandpa walter asked to be wheeled into the garage one more time. i pushed his chair and the oxygen tank rattled. he looked at his bench and asked, "is my good screwdriver still there?" i said, "it is in my toolbox." he said, "good, it is in the right place." i asked, "why did you want to come out here?" he said, "to see where i was happiest." i asked, "was it really the garage?" he said, "it was the garage with you in it." i had to turn around so he would not see me cry. he said, "i can see you crying in the window reflection." i said, "shut up, grandpa."

a junior called wren a dyke in the hallway and laughed. i walked right up and asked, "what did you say?" he said, "you heard me, emo." i said, "say it again to my face." he said it again. i hit him in the mouth and his lip split on his braces. he shoved me into the lockers and my head cracked on the metal. a teacher pulled us apart and asked, "who started this?" wren said, "he did, with a slur." the dean asked me, "was hitting him worth a suspension?" i said, "yes." he said, "three days." i said, "worth it." wren brought me ice and said, "you are insane and i love you."

a senior had a kegger in a cornfield with a bonfire and a truck blasting music. a guy at the keg asked, "you know how to do a keg stand?" i said, "no, but i know how to fall off one." two guys held my legs and i drank upside down while everybody counted and beer went up my nose. i came down choking and yelled, "twelve seconds!" somebody yelled, "the emo girl can drink!" wren asked, "are you going to puke?" i said, "not yet." at two the cops came with lights and everybody ran into the corn. i lost a boot in the mud and ran home with one sock soaked in beer and dirt.

mom saw me come in with one boot at three in the morning. she asked, "where is your other shoe?" i said, "in a cornfield." she asked, "why is it in a cornfield?" i said, "the cops came." she closed her eyes and asked, "were you arrested?" i said, "no, i am fast." she asked, "were you drinking?" i said, "yes." she asked, "did you drive?" i said, "no, i ran." she said, "good. never drive, never get in with anybody who did." i said, "i know, mom." she said, "say it back." i said, "never drive, never get in." she said, "go shower, you smell like a frat house."

after a kegger the boy with the chain wallet jingled his keys and said, "come on, i will drive you home." i asked, "how many beers?" he said, "like four." i said, "you had eight, i counted." he said, "i am fine." i grabbed the keys out of his hand and said, "you are not fine, you are a dead body with a license." he yelled, "give them back!" i threw them into the bonfire. everybody screamed. he said, "what the fuck, unity!" i said, "now nobody dies tonight." we walked four miles home and he did not talk to me. a month later a kid from another school wrapped his car around a tree drunk, and he called me crying and said thank you.

my therapist asked, "how often are you smoking now?" i said, "every night." she asked, "why every night?" i said, "because it is the only way i fall asleep." she asked, "what happens when you do not?" i said, "i lie there and my brain reads me every mistake i ever made." she said, "that sounds awful." i said, "it is. weed turns the volume down." she asked, "is it still working?" i thought and said, "less." she said, "that is how it goes." i asked, "so what do i do?" she said, "we talk to your doctor about sleep, and you try one night a week without it." i said, "one night, fine."

the first night without weed i was awake until five. i texted wren, "are you up?" she wrote, "no, i am dead, what." i wrote, "i cannot sleep without smoking." she wrote, "want to count sheep?" i wrote, "i want to kill the sheep." she wrote, "lol okay, count dead sheep." i wrote, "one dead sheep. two dead sheep." she wrote, "you are so dark, go to bed." i wrote, "forty dead sheep." she stopped answering. i fell asleep at fifty three and woke up feeling weirdly clear. i texted her, "it worked." she wrote, "i am never helping you again."

i drew my tattoo design a hundred times in my notebook. the record store manager looked over my shoulder and asked, "what is it?" i said, "a key with a heartbeat line through it." he asked, "why a key?" i said, "grandpa said to give somebody a key." he asked, "who did you give it to?" i said, "nobody yet. that is why it is on my arm." he said, "that is deep for a sixteen year old." i said, "i am deep for anybody." he asked, "when are you getting it?" i said, "the day i turn eighteen, at nine in the morning." he said, "i will close the store and come."

mom and i had not talked for a week after the shoplifting. at the laundromat she handed me a stack of quarters and said, "you do the whites." i asked, "is this a peace offering?" she said, "it is laundry." i asked, "is the laundry a peace offering?" she sighed and said, "yes." i folded her shirts and she folded mine. she asked, "are you still mad at me for being mad?" i said, "a little." she said, "i am still mad at you for stealing." i said, "fair." she said, "i love you even when i am mad." i said, "same," and put her socks together right for once.

in february the gray came back so heavy i stopped going to school for a week. my therapist asked, "are you safe?" i said, "i do not know." she asked, "do you have a plan?" i said, "no. i just keep thinking it would be easier." she said, "i think you need more help than one hour a week right now." i asked, "like the hospital?" she said, "like a day program. you go during the day and come home at night." i said, "i do not want to be a crazy person." she said, "you would be a sick person getting better." mom drove me there on monday and held my hand in the parking lot.

at the day program a girl with bandages on her wrists asked, "what are you in for?" i said, "wanting to sleep forever." she said, "same." a boy said, "i am in for panic attacks, i thought i was dying in a walmart." i said, "walmart would do it to anybody." everybody laughed, even the counselor. the counselor asked me, "what would you want to feel by the end of this?" i said, "like i have a floor again." she said, "we can work with that." on the last day the girl with the bandages hugged me and said, "stay alive, okay?" i said, "you too." we both meant it.

when i came back the boy with the chain wallet asked, "where the fuck were you for three weeks?" i said, "a program for sad kids." the table went quiet. the purple-haired girl asked, "like a mental hospital?" i said, "like a mental day camp." devon asked, "are you okay now?" i said, "better. not fixed." wren squeezed my hand under the table. the boy said, "my sister went to one of those." i asked, "did it help?" he said, "she is in college now." i said, "then maybe it works." he slid his fries over to me and said, "welcome back, freak."

the chemistry teacher asked, "why are you smiling at balancing equations?" i said, "because it is just code with atoms." she asked, "how so?" i said, "inputs on the left, outputs on the right, and nothing gets deleted, it just gets moved." she said, "that is exactly right." a boy said, "nerd." i said, "nerd who is going to get paid more than your whole family." the teacher said, "unity." i said, "sorry, nerd who is going to be very kind to his whole family." she laughed into her coffee and gave me the extra credit sheet.

a tech blog linked my post about building the mood tracker and i got four thousand visitors in a day. mom asked, "why is your phone going crazy?" i said, "people are reading my blog." she asked, "how many people?" i said, "four thousand." she screamed, "four thousand?" i said, "mom, calm down." she asked, "are any of them weird?" i said, "one asked if i am single, i deleted it." she said, "good." a programmer from a real company emailed, "impressive work, keep going." i printed it and put it on the fridge myself.

a new girl asked me, "is the goth thing a phase?" i said, "it is a decade." she asked, "do you ever wear colors?" i said, "pink, underneath, where nobody can see." she asked, "why underneath?" i said, "because the soft part is mine and the black part is for everybody else." she said, "that is kind of beautiful." i said, "do not tell anybody i said something beautiful." she asked, "can i sit with you?" i said, "if you can handle the dead table." she sat. wren whispered, "we are collecting strays." i said, "we are a shelter."

for halloween sixteen i did my whole face as a sugar skull and went to a kegger in a barn. a guy asked, "what are you supposed to be?" i said, "your future." he asked, "what does that mean?" i said, "dead, eventually." he said, "that is so dark." i said, "it is halloween, read the room." wren was dressed as a vampire and got fake blood in the keg. somebody yelled, "the beer is red!" i yelled, "it is festive!" we danced on hay bales until a cow mooed outside and half the party screamed. i laughed so hard i had to sit in the hay.

they moved grandpa walter to the hospital for good in december. i asked the nurse, "is this the last time he goes home?" she said, "he might not go home again, honey." i went in and he was so small in the bed. he whispered, "there is my engineer." i asked, "how are you?" he said, "dying, but with style." i laughed and cried at the same time. he asked, "are you still building?" i said, "every day." he said, "that is all i need to hear." i read him the comments from my blog and he whispered, "four thousand people, kiddo." i said, "four thousand and one with you."

a man in a truck yelled at me and wren at the bus stop, "hey, ladies, need a ride?" i yelled, "we are in high school, you creep!" he laughed and drove slow next to us. wren took a picture of his license plate. i asked, "what are you doing?" she said, "evidence." he sped off. at home mom asked, "what is wrong?" i told her. she took the picture and called the police non-emergency line. i asked, "will they do anything?" she said, "probably not, but now it is written down." i said, "so we write everything down." she said, "every single one."

at the end of the year i told the crew, "i am not coming to the keggers for a while." the boy with the chain wallet asked, "why?" i said, "because i woke up on a stranger's floor and i do not remember how." devon asked, "are you quitting us?" i said, "no, i am quitting blacking out." the purple-haired girl asked, "can you do that and still hang out?" i said, "we will find out." wren said, "we can do movie nights." the boy said, "movie nights are lame." i said, "so are funerals." he was quiet and then said, "okay, movie nights."

a girl in chemistry asked, "who are you going to homecoming with?" i said, "the whole dead table." she asked, "like as a group?" i said, "like as a cult." we showed up in all black, seven of us, and the purple-haired girl brought a fog machine in her backpack. a teacher asked, "is that a fog machine?" i said, "it is a mood." we danced in a circle to every sad song and stood against the wall for every happy one. devon asked, "is this the best homecoming ever?" i said, "it is the only good one." the fog set off a smoke alarm and we got kicked out at ten and ate fries in the parking lot until midnight.

a girl at the lockers asked, "so are you and devon together?" i said, "no." she asked, "then why are you always together?" i said, "because he is my best friend and he is the only person who laughs at my jokes." she said, "that is literally what a boyfriend is." i said, "no, that is what a friend is, you have just never had one." she rolled her eyes and walked off. i told devon at lunch and he asked, "do people really think that?" i said, "half the school." he said, "gross." i said, "so gross." we both laughed so hard wren asked, "what is so funny?" i said, "the school is stupid."
